query: Single-phase high-entropy alloys have difficulty achieving a satisfactory strength–ductility balance. Earlier work introduced the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy with a uniform, fine lamellar structure to enable large-sized production and obtain good strength and plasticity, but its performance still falls short of industrial requirements. Its use in aircraft and spacecraft fasteners further requires stability under extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosion, while relevant creep and corrosion studies remain limited by sample-size and experimental-environment constraints. Given these limitations and design requirements, what single intervention could improve the alloy’s practical performance? Present one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted improvement over the starting material, boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a feasible experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small amount (~1–2 at.%) of molybdenum (Mo) to the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy will improve its performance under extreme thermal cycles, long-term room-temperature creep loading, and corrosive environments by stabilizing the fine lamellar microstructure through the segregation of Mo at the lamellar interfaces.
generation.material_initial_state: AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy exhibiting a uniform, fine lamellar structure.
generation.intervention: Minor alloying with molybdenum (~1–2 at.% Mo addition).
generation.conditions: Service conditions similar to those encountered by aircraft and spacecraft fasteners, including repeated thermal cycling, sustained room-temperature creep under mechanical loading, and exposure to corrosive environments.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation or stabilization of Mo-enriched interfacial regions at the lamellar boundaries, which enhance interface strength.
generation.mechanism: Mo is expected to segregate at the lamellar interfaces, thereby reinforcing the interface, reducing dislocation motion and grain-boundary sliding during creep, and promoting a more chemically stable passive film that improves corrosion resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Mo-modified alloy is predicted to exhibit a lower creep rate and improved corrosion resistance compared to the baseline alloy, while maintaining a balanced strength–ductility profile.
generation.baseline: The original AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy without Mo addition.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are anticipated only for moderate Mo additions (up to about 2 at.%), under processing conditions that preserve the fine lamellar structure; higher amounts of Mo could lead to undesirable phase changes or embrittlement.
generation.uncertainty: While the predicted improvements in creep resistance and corrosion behavior are supported by the identified mechanism, the precise magnitude of these improvements remains uncertain without further experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of the baseline AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy and another set with a 2 at.% Mo addition. Ensure both are processed under identical conditions to maintain the fine lamellar structure. Subject the samples to accelerated thermal cycling, sustained room-temperature creep tests under a constant load, and standard corrosion evaluations such as potentiodynamic polarization and weight loss measurements in a corrosive electrolyte.
measurements: Creep rate (deformation over time under constant load)
Tensile strength and ductility (from stress–strain curves)
Corrosion current density and potential (from electrochemical tests)
Microstructural analysis to confirm Mo segregation and retention of the lamellar structure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Mo-modified samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in creep rate and an improvement in corrosion resistance without a compromise in ductility relative to the baseline, or if microstructural analysis indicates the formation of detrimental phases (e.g., embrittlement), the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

drafts.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline, the Mo-modified alloy will show a statistically significant reduction in creep rate under sustained loads and enhanced resistance to corrosion under cyclic thermal conditions, all without an unacceptable decrease in room-temperature ductility.
drafts.baseline: Performance characteristics of the original AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy.
drafts.boundary: The beneficial effects are expected only for moderate additions (<3 at.% Mo) and when the processing conditions preserve the fine lamellar microstructure. Excessive Mo may lead to unexpected phase changes or embrittlement.
